Stress is internal force per unit area. Normal stress is σ = N/A (tension positive). Shear stress τ acts tangentially to the plane. Both are measured in Pa; N/mm² = MPa is the usual working unit. Engineering normal strain is ε = δ/L₀, and shear strain γ is the change in a right angle, in radians.

Linear elasticity (Hooke's law):
- σ = Eε and τ = Gγ
- Poisson's ratio ν = −ε_lateral/ε_axial. It is about 0.3 for steel and must lie between −1 and 0.5 for an isotropic material
- For isotropic materials, G = E/[2(1 + ν)] and the bulk modulus K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)]
- Generalised Hooke's law: εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E, plus a thermal strain αΔT if the temperature changes

The tensile test gives the proportional limit, the yield stress σy (or the 0.2% proof stress for metals without a clear yield point), the ultimate tensile strength, and ductility measured by elongation and reduction of area. The area under the elastic part of the curve is the modulus of resilience, σy²/(2E).

Plane stress transformation. On a plane at θ:
- σ_θ = (σx + σy)/2 + [(σx − σy)/2] cos 2θ + τxy sin 2θ
- Principal stresses: σ₁,₂ = (σx + σy)/2 ± √{[(σx − σy)/2]² + τxy²}
- Principal planes: tan 2θp = 2τxy/(σx − σy). The shear stress on these planes is zero
- Maximum in-plane shear stress equals the radius R of Mohr's circle, on planes at 45° to the principal planes
Mohr's circle is centred at ((σx + σy)/2, 0) with radius R. A rotation of θ on the element is 2θ on the circle.

Yield criteria for ductile metals:
- Tresca (maximum shear): yield when σmax − σmin = σy. Remember to include σ₃ = 0 in plane stress
- von Mises (distortion energy): σvm = √(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²) in plane stress, with yield when σvm = σy
Tresca is slightly more conservative. Brittle materials are better described by maximum normal stress (Rankine) or Mohr–Coulomb criteria.

Worked example. With σx = 80 MPa, σy = −20 MPa and τxy = 30 MPa: the centre is at 30 MPa and R = √(50² + 30²) = 58.3 MPa. So σ₁ = 88.3 MPa, σ₂ = −28.3 MPa, θp = 15.5°, and τmax(in-plane) = 58.3 MPa.

Common pitfalls:
- Forgetting the factor of 2 in angles on Mohr's circle
- Ignoring the out-of-plane principal stress (zero) when finding the absolute maximum shear
- Unit slips between mm² and m². 1 MPa = 1 N/mm²
- Applying G = E/[2(1 + ν)] to anisotropic materials such as timber or composites

For a prismatic bar in tension or compression, σ = P/A and the elongation is δ = PL/(AE). Saint-Venant's principle says that stress concentrations near loads and supports die away within about one bar width, so the uniform-stress formula holds away from the ends.

Bars with segments: δ = Σ PᵢLᵢ/(AᵢEᵢ). Find each segment's internal force Pᵢ from a free-body diagram of the bar on one side of a cut. With a varying area or load, δ = ∫ P(x) dx/[A(x)E]. A hanging bar under its own weight stretches by ρgL²/(2E), which is half the stretch that the same total weight would cause if applied at the end.

Statically indeterminate axial problems need three ingredients:
- Equilibrium (not enough equations by itself)
- Compatibility: how the deformations are geometrically related
- Force–deformation relations: δ = PL/(AE) + αΔT L
Typical cases are a bar fixed at both ends, a concrete column with steel reinforcement, and a rigid bar hung from several wires.

Composite (parallel) members have equal strains, so the load divides in proportion to AE. For a steel-reinforced concrete column, σs/σc = Es/Ec, which is the modular ratio n. An equivalent (transformed) area is A_c + nA_s.

Thermal stress. A bar fully restrained against expansion has σ = −EαΔT, whatever its length or area. For steel (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C), a 40 °C temperature rise gives 96 MPa in compression. In a compound bar of two materials heated together, the one with the higher α ends up in compression and the other in tension. Their forces are equal and opposite.

Strain energy in axial loading: U = P²L/(2AE). Under elastic conditions, a suddenly applied load (dropped from zero height) produces twice the static stress.

Stress concentrations. Holes, fillets and notches raise the local peak stress: σmax = Kt σnom. Kt is about 3 for a small circular hole in a wide plate. This matters for fatigue and brittle materials. A ductile material under static load redistributes stress by local yielding.

Worked example. A steel bar (E = 200 GPa) has a 600 mm² segment 800 mm long and a 300 mm² segment 500 mm long, and carries 60 kN. δ = (60,000/200,000) × (800/600 + 500/300) = 0.3 × 3.0 = 0.90 mm.

Common pitfalls:
- Using the total load in every segment instead of the internal force found from a cut
- Sign errors in compatibility. Draw the deformed shape first
- Forgetting that thermal strain is stress-free when the bar is unrestrained
- Mixing mm and m in PL/(AE)

For a circular shaft (solid or hollow) under torque T, elastic theory assumes that plane sections stay plane and radii stay straight. That gives the torsion formula:
τ/r = T/J = Gθ/L
- τ = Tr/J. The shear stress varies linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the outer surface
- θ = TL/(GJ) is the angle of twist in radians. GJ/L is the torsional stiffness
- Polar second moment of area: J = πd⁴/32 for a solid shaft, and J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32 for a hollow one
- Solid shaft: τmax = 16T/(πd³)

Power transmission: P = Tω, with ω = 2πN/60 for N in rev/min. A shaft delivering 50 kW at 1200 rev/min carries T = 50,000/125.66 = 398 N m. With an allowable stress of 60 MPa, d = (16T/πτ)^(1/3) = 32.3 mm, so choose a standard size of 35 mm.

Hollow shafts work better per unit mass, because material near the axis carries little stress. For the same maximum stress and torque, a hollow shaft with d/D = 0.67 uses roughly two-thirds of the material of a solid one.

Shafts in series (segments end to end) carry the same torque, and their twists add. Shafts in parallel (both fixed ends, or geared together) share the torque. Compatibility gives equal twist, or angles related by the gear ratio. For a shaft fixed at both ends with torque T₀ applied at an intermediate point, T_A + T_B = T₀ and θ_A = θ_B.

Stress state. Pure torsion gives pure shear at the surface. The principal stresses ±τ act at 45° to the shaft axis. Brittle materials such as chalk or cast iron therefore fracture on a 45° helix. Ductile materials fail on a transverse plane, where the shear is greatest.

Combined bending and torsion of a solid shaft:
- Tresca equivalent torque: T_e = √(M² + T²)
- von Mises equivalent moment: M_e = √(M² + 0.75T²)
- Then τmax = 16T_e/(πd³), or σ_vm = 32M_e/(πd³)

Non-circular sections warp, so the simple formula does not apply. For thin-walled closed tubes, use Bredt–Batho: τ = T/(2A_m t), where A_m is the area enclosed by the mid-line of the wall. Open thin sections (channels, angles) are far less stiff in torsion than closed sections.

Common pitfalls:
- Using rev/min directly in P = Tω
- Using I (= πd⁴/64) instead of J
- Leaving θ in radians when the question asks for degrees, or the reverse
- Applying circular-shaft formulas to rectangular bars
- Forgetting that series segments carry the same torque

Shear force and bending moment diagrams come first. Take sections and use equilibrium of one side. Use a consistent convention: sagging moment positive, and shear positive when it tends to rotate the element clockwise. The key relations are:
- dV/dx = −w (w is the downward distributed load)
- dM/dx = V
- So M is a maximum or minimum where V = 0 or changes sign
- A point load causes a jump in V. An applied couple causes a jump in M
- The change in M between two points equals the area of the shear force diagram between them

Standard results: simply supported span L with a central load P gives Mmax = PL/4. A uniformly distributed load w gives Mmax = wL²/8. A cantilever with an end load gives M = PL at the root.

Simple bending theory (Euler–Bernoulli) assumes that plane sections remain plane and normal to the neutral axis, the material is linear elastic, and E is the same in tension and compression. Then:
σ/y = M/I = E/R
- σ = My/I. The stress varies linearly with distance y from the neutral axis, which passes through the centroid
- Section modulus Z = I/y_max, so σmax = M/Z
- Rectangle: I = bd³/12 and Z = bd²/6. Solid circle: I = πd⁴/64
- Parallel-axis theorem: I = Σ(I_c + A h²) for composite sections

For unsymmetrical sections (T or channel), the neutral axis is not at mid-depth, so the extreme tensile and compressive stresses differ. Cast iron T-beams, weak in tension, put the flange on the tension side.

Worked example. A T-section has a 120 × 20 mm flange on a 100 × 20 mm web, and overall depth 120 mm.
- Centroid from the bottom of the web: ȳ = (2400 × 110 + 2000 × 50)/4400 = 82.7 mm
- I = 120(20)³/12 + 2400(27.3)² + 20(100)³/12 + 2000(32.7)² = 5.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴
- Under a sagging M of 5.625 kN m, the top flange is in compression at 5.625 × 10⁶ × 37.3/I = 37.0 MPa, and the bottom of the web is in tension at 82.0 MPa

Composite beams use the transformed-section method (scale widths by n = E₂/E₁). Plastic bending: the plastic moment is Mp = σy Zp, and the shape factor Zp/Ze is 1.5 for a rectangle and about 1.15 for I-sections.

Common pitfalls:
- Taking y from the top or bottom instead of from the neutral axis
- Using I about the wrong axis
- Sign slips at point loads
- Assuming Mmax is always at midspan
- Mixing kN m with mm units. Convert M to N mm

Where the bending moment varies, horizontal shear must act between the fibres. Equilibrium of a slice gives the shear flow and shear stress formulas:
q = VQ/I and τ = VQ/(Ib)
- V is the shear force at the section
- Q = A′ȳ′ is the first moment, about the neutral axis, of the area beyond the level being considered
- b is the width of the section at that level
- Shear flow q (N/mm) is the shear force per unit length along the beam

Distributions to know:
- Rectangle: parabolic, zero at the top and bottom faces. τmax = 1.5V/A at the neutral axis
- Solid circle: τmax = (4/3)V/A
- I-section: the web carries most of the vertical shear, at a nearly uniform τ ≈ V/A_web. The flanges carry shear flow horizontally. There is a jump in τ where the width changes from flange to web

Built-up beams. Nails, bolts or welds joining parts of a section must carry the shear flow at the interface. Spacing s = F_connector/q, where q = VQ/I and Q is the first moment of the part being held on. With two rows of nails, each nail carries q·s/2.

Shear centre. For a section with only one axis of symmetry (a channel, for example), a transverse load produces bending without twist only if it passes through the shear centre. For a thin channel of flange width b, web height h and uniform thickness, the shear centre lies e = 3b²/(h + 6b) behind the web centre line, on the side away from the flanges.

When shear matters:
- Short, heavily loaded beams and beams with thin webs (which risk web shear buckling)
- Timber, which is weak in horizontal shear along the grain
- Connections in built-up and composite beams
- Shear deflection of deep beams
For long slender beams, bending stress usually governs.

Worked example. A T-beam is made of a 150 × 50 mm flange nailed to a 50 × 150 mm web, and V = 2 kN.
- Centroid: 125 mm from the bottom, so I = 53.1 × 10⁶ mm⁴
- Q of the flange = 7500 × 50 = 375 × 10³ mm³
- q = 2000 × 375,000/53.1 × 10⁶ = 14.1 N/mm
- With nails rated at 800 N each, s = 800/14.1 = 56 mm

Common pitfalls:
- Using the full section area in Q, or measuring ȳ′ from the base instead of the neutral axis
- Using the flange width b when finding τ in the web
- Forgetting that τ is zero at free surfaces
- Confusing shear flow (N/mm) with shear stress (N/mm²)

The elastic curve satisfies EI d²y/dx² = M(x), with y measured upwards and sagging M positive. The slope is θ = dy/dx, and further derivatives relate EI y‴ to V and EI y⁗ to −w. The theory assumes small slopes and neglects shear deformation.

Double integration: integrate M/EI twice and find the constants from the boundary conditions.
- Simple support: y = 0
- Fixed end: y = 0 and dy/dx = 0
- Free end: M = 0 and V = 0 (already built into M(x))

Macaulay's method handles discontinuous loading with one expression. Write M with bracket terms ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ, which are zero when x < a. Integrate the brackets as whole units, so that a single pair of constants holds over the whole span. For a uniform load that stops before the end of the beam, add an equal and opposite load to the end so the terms continue. Couples appear as M₀⟨x − a⟩⁰.

Standard results to know:
- Cantilever, end load P: δ = PL³/(3EI), θ = PL²/(2EI)
- Cantilever, uniform load w: δ = wL⁴/(8EI)
- Simply supported, central P: δ = PL³/(48EI)
- Simply supported, uniform load w: δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI)

Moment–area theorems:
- The change in slope between A and B equals the area of the M/EI diagram between them
- The tangential deviation of B from the tangent at A equals the first moment of that area about B
These are quick for cantilevers and symmetric beams.

Superposition: add the deflections from separate standard cases. This holds because the response is linear.

Statically indeterminate beams. Remove a redundant reaction, find the deflection at that point from the load and from the redundant separately, and impose compatibility (usually zero deflection at the support). A propped cantilever with a uniform load has a prop reaction of 3wL/8, a fixed-end moment of wL²/8, and a maximum sagging moment of 9wL²/128 at 3L/8 from the prop.

Worked example. A simply supported 5 m beam carries 20 kN at 2 m from A, with EI = 8000 kN m².
- R_A = 12 kN, so EI y = 2x³ − (10/3)⟨x − 2⟩³ + C₁x
- y(5) = 0 gives C₁ = −32 kN m²
- Under the load: y = (16 − 64)/8000 = −6.0 mm
- The maximum, 6.17 mm, occurs at x = √[(L² − a²)/3] measured from the support further from the load, which is 2.65 m from B (2.35 m from A)

Common pitfalls:
- Expanding Macaulay brackets
- Wrong boundary conditions
- Units: EI in N mm² with loads in kN
- Assuming the maximum deflection is under the load
- Forgetting the sign convention for y

Slender compression members can fail by elastic instability at stresses well below yield. Buckling is a stability failure: at the critical load, a neighbouring bent equilibrium position becomes possible.

Euler critical load for an ideal (perfectly straight, centrally loaded, linear elastic) pin-ended column:
P_cr = π²EI/L²

For other end conditions, use the effective length L_e = KL:
- Pinned–pinned: K = 1
- Fixed–free (flagpole): K = 2
- Fixed–pinned: K ≈ 0.7
- Fixed–fixed: K = 0.5
Then P_cr = π²EI/L_e². Real end fixity is never perfect, so design codes recommend somewhat larger K values than these theoretical ones.

Slenderness ratio λ = L_e/r, where r = √(I/A) is the radius of gyration. The Euler stress is σ_cr = π²E/λ². Buckling occurs about the axis with the smallest r, unless the restraints differ between axes. If they differ, check both axes, each with its own effective length.

Limits of Euler theory. Euler applies only while σ_cr is below the proportional limit. The transition slenderness is λ = π√(E/σy), about 89 for steel with σy = 250 MPa. Stockier columns fail by inelastic buckling or by crushing.

Real columns have initial crookedness, eccentric loading and residual stresses, so they fail below both the Euler and squash loads, most noticeably near the transition. Models for this include:
- Rankine–Gordon: 1/P = 1/P_squash + 1/P_Euler, an empirical blend
- Perry–Robertson: an initial-imperfection model, which forms the basis of the European column curves in Eurocode 3
- Secant formula: for a known load eccentricity e

Thermal buckling. A restrained bar heated by ΔT develops P = EAαΔT. It buckles when this reaches P_cr, so the critical temperature rise is ΔT_cr = π²r²/(αL_e²). Rail tracks have expansion gaps or prestressed welded rail for this reason.

Worked example. A 40 mm diameter solid steel strut, 2 m long and pinned at both ends (E = 200 GPa):
- I = π(40)⁴/64 = 1.257 × 10⁵ mm⁴
- P_cr = π² × 200,000 × 1.257 × 10⁵/2000² = 62.0 kN
- σ_cr = 49 MPa, well below yield
- λ = 2000/10 = 200. The strut is slender, so Euler is valid

Common pitfalls:
- Using I_max instead of I_min
- Using the actual length instead of the effective length
- Applying Euler to stocky members
- Unit errors with I in mm⁴
- Treating P_cr as a safe working load without a safety or imperfection factor

Determinacy:
- Plane pin-jointed frame: m + r versus 2j
- Plane rigid-jointed frame: degree of indeterminacy = 3m + r − 3j, with adjustments for internal pins or releases
Determinate structures can be solved by statics, and settlement or temperature changes cause no stress in them. Indeterminate structures need compatibility, but they redistribute load and have reserves of strength.

Energy methods:
- Strain energy: axial U = ΣN²L/(2AE), bending U = ∫M²dx/(2EI), torsion U = ∫T²dx/(2GJ)
- Castigliano's second theorem: the deflection at a load P is δ = ∂U/∂P. For a deflection where no load acts, add a dummy load and set it to zero at the end
- Unit load method (virtual work): truss joint deflection δ = Σ N n L/(AE), where N is the member force under the real loads and n is the member force under a unit load at the point and in the direction wanted. For beams and frames, δ = ∫ M m dx/(EI)

Indeterminate structures:
- Flexibility (force) method: release redundants, find the gaps they leave, and close them with compatibility equations
- Stiffness (displacement) method: unknowns are the joint displacements, and member stiffnesses are assembled into a global matrix, [K]{d} = {F}. This is the basis of matrix and finite element software
- Moment distribution (Hardy Cross, 1930): an iterative hand method for continuous beams and frames, using fixed-end moments, distribution factors (proportional to member stiffness, 4EI/L or 3EI/L) and carry-over factors (½ to a fixed far end)
- Slope-deflection equations: a hand version of the stiffness method

Influence lines show how a reaction or internal force at a fixed point varies as a unit load moves across the structure. They are used to place moving loads in bridges for the worst case. The Müller-Breslau principle states that the influence line has the shape of the deflected structure when the corresponding restraint is released and given a unit displacement.

Plastic collapse. Assume hinges form at Mp and equate external and internal work for each possible mechanism. The upper-bound theorem says that any mechanism gives a collapse load at least as large as the true value.

Worked example. A two-span continuous beam with equal spans L and a uniform load w has a central support reaction of 1.25wL, end reactions of 0.375wL, and a hogging moment of wL²/8 over the centre support.

Common pitfalls:
- Mixing the sign conventions for N and n in the unit load method
- Forgetting the units of AE
- Using 4EI/L instead of 3EI/L for a member pinned at its far end in moment distribution
- Treating indeterminate structures as if one load path carried everything

cards.f: Define engineering normal stress and strain.
cards.b: Stress σ = N/A₀ (internal normal force over the original area). Strain ε = δ/L₀ (change in length over the original length), which is dimensionless.

cards.f: Define Poisson's ratio and give its theoretical range for isotropic materials.
cards.b: ν = −ε_lateral/ε_axial. For a stable isotropic material it lies between −1 and 0.5. It is about 0.3 for steel and close to 0.5 for rubber, which is nearly incompressible.

cards.f: How are E, G and ν related for an isotropic material?
cards.b: G = E/[2(1 + ν)]. For steel, with E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3, G ≈ 77 GPa.

cards.f: Give the principal stresses in plane stress.
cards.b: σ₁,₂ = (σx + σy)/2 ± √{[(σx − σy)/2]² + τxy²}. They act on planes where the shear stress is zero, at tan 2θp = 2τxy/(σx − σy).

cards.f: What do the centre and radius of Mohr's circle represent?
cards.b: The centre is the average normal stress (σx + σy)/2. The radius equals the maximum in-plane shear stress. A rotation of θ on the element is 2θ on the circle.

cards.f: State the Tresca yield criterion.
cards.b: Yield occurs when the maximum shear stress reaches σy/2, that is when σmax − σmin = σy. In plane stress, include σ₃ = 0 when choosing σmax and σmin.

cards.f: State the von Mises criterion for plane stress.
cards.b: σvm = √(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²) = √(σx² − σxσy + σy² + 3τxy²). Yield is predicted when σvm = σy. It is based on distortion energy.

cards.f: What is the 0.2% proof stress?
cards.b: The stress at which a line drawn parallel to the elastic part of the curve, offset by 0.2% strain, meets the stress–strain curve. It is used as the yield strength for metals with no clear yield point, such as aluminium.

cards.f: Write the generalised Hooke's law for εx, including temperature.
cards.b: εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E + αΔT.

cards.f: Give the elongation of a bar made of segments under axial load.
cards.b: δ = Σ PᵢLᵢ/(AᵢEᵢ), where Pᵢ is the internal force in segment i, found from a free-body diagram cut through that segment.

cards.f: What three sets of equations solve a statically indeterminate axial problem?
cards.b: Equilibrium, compatibility of deformations, and force–deformation relations (δ = PL/AE + αΔT L).

cards.f: What stress develops in a fully restrained bar heated by ΔT?
cards.b: σ = −EαΔT (compressive), independent of length and area. For steel and ΔT = 40 °C: 200,000 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 40 = 96 MPa.

cards.f: How is load shared in a parallel composite member, such as a reinforced concrete column?
cards.b: The parts have equal strain, so each carries load in proportion to its AE. The stress ratio equals the modular ratio: σs/σc = Es/Ec.

cards.f: State Saint-Venant's principle.
cards.b: The effect of how a load is applied dies away within about one characteristic width of the member. Further away, the stress depends only on the resultant force.

cards.f: How much does a uniform bar hanging under its own weight stretch?
cards.b: δ = ρgL²/(2E). That is half the stretch caused by the same total weight hung at the free end.

cards.f: Compare the stress from a suddenly applied load with that from a gradually applied one.
cards.b: A load applied suddenly (with no drop height) to a linear elastic bar causes a peak stress twice the static value.

cards.f: What is a stress concentration factor?
cards.b: Kt = σmax/σnom, the ratio of the local peak stress at a notch, hole or fillet to the nominal stress. For a small circular hole in a wide plate under tension, Kt ≈ 3.

cards.f: In a compound bar of steel and aluminium heated together, which part is in compression?
cards.b: Aluminium, because it has the larger α and is held back by the steel. The steel is pulled into tension, and the two forces are equal and opposite.

cards.f: State the torsion formula for circular shafts.
cards.b: τ/r = T/J = Gθ/L. The shear stress varies linearly with radius and is greatest at the outer surface.

cards.f: Give J for solid and hollow circular shafts.
cards.b: Solid: J = πd⁴/32. Hollow: J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32. J is twice the second moment of area I about a diameter.

cards.f: How do you find shaft torque from power and speed?
cards.b: T = P/ω, with ω = 2πN/60 rad/s for N in rev/min. For example, 50 kW at 1200 rev/min gives T = 398 N m.

cards.f: Give the maximum shear stress in a solid shaft.
cards.b: τmax = 16T/(πd³).

cards.f: Why does a cast iron or chalk bar in torsion break on a 45° helix?
cards.b: Pure shear gives principal stresses ±τ at 45° to the axis. Brittle materials fail in tension, so they fracture normal to σ₁, along a helix.

cards.f: Why are hollow shafts more efficient than solid ones?
cards.b: Material near the axis is lightly stressed and adds little to J. Removing it saves a lot of mass for a small loss of strength and stiffness.

cards.f: State the Bredt–Batho formula.
cards.b: For a thin-walled closed tube, τ = T/(2A_m t), where A_m is the area enclosed by the wall's mid-line and t is the local wall thickness. The shear flow q = τt is constant around the tube.

cards.f: Give the equivalent torque and moment for combined bending and torsion of a solid shaft.
cards.b: Tresca: T_e = √(M² + T²), so τmax = 16T_e/(πd³). von Mises: M_e = √(M² + 0.75T²), so σ_vm = 32M_e/(πd³).

cards.f: How are shafts in series and in parallel handled?
cards.b: In series, the segments carry the same torque and their twists add. In parallel (for example, fixed at both ends), the torques add to the applied torque and the twists are equal.

cards.f: State the simple bending equation.
cards.b: σ/y = M/I = E/R, where y is measured from the neutral axis, I is the second moment of area about it, and R is the radius of curvature.

cards.f: What are the differential relations between load, shear and moment?
cards.b: dV/dx = −w and dM/dx = V. Maximum moment occurs where the shear force is zero or changes sign.

cards.f: Give I and Z for a rectangular section b × d about its centroidal axis.
cards.b: I = bd³/12 and Z = bd²/6.

cards.f: Where does the neutral axis lie in elastic bending?
cards.b: It passes through the centroid of the cross-section, provided the material is homogeneous and linear elastic with equal E in tension and compression.

cards.f: Give Mmax for a simply supported beam with a central point load and with a uniform load.
cards.b: Central point load P: PL/4. Uniform load w: wL²/8. Both occur at midspan.

cards.f: Why should a cast iron T-beam be placed with its flange on the tension side?
cards.b: Cast iron is much weaker in tension. The neutral axis lies close to the flange, so the flange fibres have the smaller y and the lower stress. Putting the flange in tension keeps the tensile stress low.

cards.f: What is the shape factor of a section?
cards.b: The ratio of the plastic modulus to the elastic modulus, Zp/Ze. It is 1.5 for a rectangle, 1.7 for a solid circle and about 1.15 for typical I-sections.

cards.f: How does the transformed-section method work for composite beams?
cards.b: Choose one reference material and scale the width of the other by the modular ratio n = E₂/E₁. Analyse the transformed section as homogeneous, then multiply the stresses in the scaled material by n.

cards.f: What does a point load do to the shear force diagram, and an applied couple to the bending moment diagram?
cards.b: A point load causes a step in V equal to the load. An applied couple causes a step in M equal to the couple.

cards.f: State the shear stress formula for beams.
cards.b: τ = VQ/(Ib), where Q is the first moment about the neutral axis of the area beyond the level considered, and b is the width at that level.

cards.f: What is the maximum shear stress in a rectangular section?
cards.b: τmax = 1.5V/A at the neutral axis. The distribution is parabolic, with zero at the top and bottom faces.

cards.f: What is the maximum shear stress in a solid circular section?
cards.b: τmax = (4/3)V/A at the neutral axis.

cards.f: Define shear flow and give its formula.
cards.b: Shear flow is the shear force per unit length along the beam: q = VQ/I, in N/mm. It is used to design nails, bolts and welds.

cards.f: How is nail spacing in a built-up beam determined?
cards.b: s = n × F_nail/q, where n is the number of nails at each position along the beam (the number of rows), q = VQ/I, and Q is for the part being held on by the nails.

cards.f: What is the shear centre?
cards.b: The point through which a transverse load must act to cause bending without twisting. It lies on any axis of symmetry, and for a channel it lies outside the web.

cards.f: Where is the shear centre of a thin channel with uniform thickness?
cards.b: At e = 3b²/(h + 6b) behind the web centre line, on the side away from the flanges. b is the flange width and h the web height, both measured to the centre lines.

cards.f: Why does the web of an I-beam carry most of the vertical shear?
cards.b: The vertical shear stress in the flanges is small because they are wide and close to the extreme fibres, where Q is small. The web carries nearly uniform shear of about V/A_web.

cards.f: Why is horizontal shear critical in timber beams?
cards.b: Timber is weak in shear parallel to the grain. Short, deep, heavily loaded timber beams can split along the neutral axis before the bending stress is reached.

cards.f: State the differential equation of the elastic curve.
cards.b: EI d²y/dx² = M(x), with y positive upwards and sagging M positive. It assumes small slopes and neglects shear deformation.

cards.f: Give the tip deflection of a cantilever with an end load and with a uniform load.
cards.b: End load P: PL³/(3EI). Uniform load w: wL⁴/(8EI).

cards.f: Give the midspan deflection of a simply supported beam with a central load and with a uniform load.
cards.b: Central load P: PL³/(48EI). Uniform load w: 5wL⁴/(384EI).

cards.f: What is the key rule for integrating Macaulay brackets?
cards.b: Integrate ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ as a single unit, giving ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1). Never expand the bracket. The term is zero when x < a.

cards.f: How do you handle a uniform load that stops before the end of the beam in Macaulay's method?
cards.b: Continue the load to the end of the beam and add an equal upward load over the extra length, so that all bracket terms run to the end.

cards.f: State the two moment-area theorems.
cards.b: (1) The change in slope between A and B equals the area of the M/EI diagram between them. (2) The deviation of B from the tangent at A equals the first moment of that area about B.

cards.f: Give the boundary conditions at a fixed end and at a simple support.
cards.b: Fixed end: y = 0 and dy/dx = 0. Simple support: y = 0, with M = 0 if it is the end of the beam.

cards.f: Give the prop reaction of a propped cantilever with a uniform load.
cards.b: R = 3wL/8 at the prop. The fixed-end moment is wL²/8, and the maximum sagging moment is 9wL²/128 at 3L/8 from the prop.

cards.f: Why is superposition valid for beam deflections?
cards.b: The governing equations are linear when slopes are small and the material is linear elastic. Deflections from separate loads can therefore simply be added.

cards.f: State Euler's critical load for a pin-ended column.
cards.b: P_cr = π²EI/L², using the minimum second moment of area I.

cards.f: Give the effective length factors for the four classic end conditions.
cards.b: Pinned–pinned 1.0, fixed–free 2.0, fixed–pinned about 0.7, fixed–fixed 0.5. Then P_cr = π²EI/(KL)².

cards.f: Define the slenderness ratio.
cards.b: λ = L_e/r, where r = √(I/A) is the least radius of gyration. The Euler stress is σ_cr = π²E/λ².

cards.f: When is Euler's formula not valid?
cards.b: When σ_cr would exceed the proportional limit, that is when λ < π√(E/σy) (about 89 for steel with σy = 250 MPa). Stocky columns yield or buckle inelastically first.

cards.f: State the Rankine–Gordon formula.
cards.b: 1/P = 1/P_c + 1/P_E, where P_c is the squash (crushing) load and P_E the Euler load. It is an empirical blend for intermediate columns.

cards.f: Why do real columns fail below the Euler load?
cards.b: Initial crookedness, eccentric loading and residual stresses cause bending from the start, so the extreme fibres yield before P_E is reached. This is the basis of the Perry–Robertson approach.

cards.f: A rectangular strut is braced at mid-height about its weak axis only. How do you check it?
cards.b: Find P_cr about each axis with its own effective length (half the length about the weak axis, the full length about the strong axis). The smaller value governs.

cards.f: Give the critical temperature rise for thermal buckling of a restrained bar.
cards.b: ΔT_cr = π²r²/(αL_e²), found by setting EAαΔT equal to π²EI/L_e².

cards.f: Is buckling a strength failure or a stability failure?
cards.b: A stability failure. At P_cr a bent equilibrium shape becomes possible, and the column deflects sideways even though the material has not yielded.

cards.f: Give the degree of indeterminacy of a plane rigid-jointed frame.
cards.b: i = 3m + r − 3j (m members, r reactions, j joints), reduced by any internal releases such as hinges.

cards.f: State Castigliano's second theorem.
cards.b: For a linear elastic structure, the displacement at a load P in its direction is δ = ∂U/∂P. Add a dummy load where no load acts, then set it to zero.

cards.f: Give the unit load formula for truss joint deflection.
cards.b: δ = Σ NnL/(AE), where N is the member force under the real loads and n the member force under a unit load applied in the direction of the displacement wanted.

cards.f: How does the flexibility (force) method work?
cards.b: Release redundants to make the structure determinate, find the displacements at those releases, and solve compatibility equations so that the released displacements match the real supports.

cards.f: What is the stiffness method, and why is it used in software?
cards.b: The unknowns are the joint displacements. Member stiffness matrices are assembled into [K]{d} = {F}. The procedure is systematic and easy to program, which makes it the basis of frame and finite element software.

cards.f: Give the distribution and carry-over factors in moment distribution.
cards.b: Distribution factor = member stiffness ÷ total stiffness at the joint, using 4EI/L for a fixed far end and 3EI/L for a pinned far end. The carry-over factor is ½ to a fixed far end and 0 to a pinned one.

cards.f: What does the Müller-Breslau principle state?
cards.b: The influence line for a reaction or internal force has the shape of the deflected structure when that restraint is released and given a unit displacement in its direction.

cards.f: What is an influence line used for?
cards.b: It shows how a reaction, shear or moment at a fixed section varies as a unit load moves across the structure. Designers use it to place moving loads, such as on bridges, for the worst effect.

cards.f: Why do settlement and temperature change cause no stress in determinate structures?
cards.b: A determinate structure can deform freely to accommodate them without breaking compatibility, so equilibrium is still met with zero internal forces. Indeterminate structures develop stresses instead.

questions.q: A material has E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.25. Assuming it is isotropic, what is its shear modulus G?
On Mohr's circle for plane stress, the points representing two planes through a point are 30° apart. What is the angle between those planes on the physical element?
questions.why: Angles on Mohr's circle are twice the physical angles, so 30° on the circle corresponds to 15° on the element. (Principal planes are always 180° apart on the circle, i.e. 90° apart physically.)

questions.q: A steel rod carries a fixed axial load. If its diameter is doubled and its length stays the same, what happens to its elongation?
questions.why: δ = PL/(AE), and A is proportional to d², so doubling d multiplies A by 4 and divides δ by 4.

questions.q: For the same applied torque, a solid shaft's diameter is doubled. What happens to its maximum shear stress and its angle of twist?
questions.why: τmax = 16T/(πd³) scales with 1/d³, and θ = TL/(GJ) with J ∝ d⁴ scales with 1/d⁴.

questions.q: In the elastic bending of a homogeneous beam, where does the neutral axis lie?
options: Through the centroid of the cross-section
At the point of maximum shear stress, wherever that is
questions.why: Zero net axial force requires ∫y dA = 0, which locates the neutral axis at the centroid. For unsymmetrical sections this is not at mid-depth.

questions.q: A 100 mm × 200 mm rectangular timber joist carries a bending moment of 20 kN m. How do the maximum bending stresses compare when the 200 mm side is vertical and when it is horizontal?
questions.why: Upright, Z = 100 × 200²/6 = 666,667 mm³, giving 30 MPa. Flat, Z = 200 × 100²/6 = 333,333 mm³, giving 60 MPa. Depth counts as the square in Z.

questions.q: What is the ratio of maximum to average shear stress in a solid rectangular beam section?
questions.why: τmax = 1.5V/A, at the neutral axis. The ratio 4/3 applies to a solid circular section.

questions.q: A simply supported beam carries a uniformly distributed load. If the span doubles while the load intensity w and EI stay the same, by what factor does the midspan deflection increase?
questions.why: δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI), so doubling L multiplies δ by 2⁴ = 16.

questions.q: Compared with the same column pinned at both ends, what is the Euler buckling load of a column fixed at both ends?
questions.why: The effective length is 0.5L, and P_cr ∝ 1/L_e², so the load is 1/0.5² = 4 times higher.

questions.q: A steel strut (E = 200 GPa, σy = 300 MPa) has a slenderness ratio of 60. What can you conclude about the Euler formula?
options: It is valid, because Euler applies to all slender struts
It overestimates the failure load, because σ_cr from Euler (548 MPa) exceeds yield
It underestimates the failure load, because λ is below 100
It gives the squash load exactly
questions.why: σ_cr = π²E/λ² = π² × 200,000/3600 = 548 MPa, which is above σy. The transition slenderness π√(E/σy) is about 81, and λ = 60 is below it, so the strut fails by yielding or inelastic buckling before the Euler load.

questions.q: A propped cantilever (fixed at one end, simply supported at the other) carries vertical loads. What is its degree of static indeterminacy?
questions.why: There are four reaction components (three at the fixed end and one at the prop) and three equilibrium equations, so the beam is indeterminate to the first degree.

questions.q: A steel bar of 20 mm diameter carries an axial tensile load of 50 kN. Taking E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3, find the axial stress, the axial strain and the change in diameter.
markScheme: Lateral strain −νε = −2.39 × 10⁻⁴, so Δd = −0.0048 mm (a decrease of about 4.8 μm)
questions.modelAnswer: The area is A = π × 20²/4 = 314.2 mm², so the stress is σ = 50,000/314.2 = 159 MPa, which is within the elastic range for structural steel. The axial strain is ε = σ/E = 159/200,000 = 7.96 × 10⁻⁴. The lateral strain is −νε = −0.3 × 7.96 × 10⁻⁴ = −2.39 × 10⁻⁴. The diameter therefore shrinks by 2.39 × 10⁻⁴ × 20 = 0.0048 mm, about 4.8 μm.

questions.q: A cylindrical air receiver has an internal diameter of 1.2 m and a wall thickness of 10 mm, and holds a gauge pressure of 2 MPa. Using thin-wall theory, find the hoop and longitudinal stresses, and explain why longitudinal welds are the more critical ones.
markScheme: Longitudinal seams carry the hoop stress, twice the longitudinal stress, so their weld efficiency matters more
questions.modelAnswer: Thin-wall theory is reasonable because d/t = 1200/10 = 120, much more than about 20. Equilibrium of half the cylinder gives the hoop stress σ_h = pd/(2t) = 2 × 1200/(2 × 10) = 120 MPa. Equilibrium of the end cap gives the longitudinal stress σ_L = pd/(4t) = 60 MPa. A longitudinal weld runs along the length of the vessel, so the hoop stress acts across it. That stress is twice the longitudinal stress, so a defect or low weld efficiency in a longitudinal seam is the more serious risk.

questions.q: A steel rail section is fixed rigidly between two abutments at 15 °C. Find the stress in the rail when the temperature reaches 55 °C. Take E = 200 GPa and α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C. Does the length of the rail matter?
markScheme: The stress is compressive and independent of length (and area)
questions.modelAnswer: With full restraint, the free thermal strain αΔT must be cancelled by an equal and opposite mechanical strain. The stress is σ = −EαΔT = −200,000 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 40 = −96 MPa, which is 96 MPa compression. Length and cross-section cancel out, so a short rail and a long rail develop the same stress. A long rail, however, is much more likely to buckle under this compressive force.

questions.q: A stepped steel bar (E = 200 GPa) has a 600 mm² segment 800 mm long and a 300 mm² segment 500 mm long. Equal and opposite axial forces of 60 kN pull on its ends. Find the stress in each segment and the total elongation.
markScheme: The internal force is 60 kN in both segments
Notes that the smaller segment is closer to yield and governs the design
questions.modelAnswer: A cut anywhere in the bar shows an internal force of 60 kN, because the end loads are equal and opposite. The stresses are 60,000/600 = 100 MPa in the larger segment and 60,000/300 = 200 MPa in the smaller one. The elongations are 60,000 × 800/(600 × 200,000) = 0.40 mm and 60,000 × 500/(300 × 200,000) = 0.50 mm, so the total is 0.90 mm. The thinner segment is more highly stressed and would govern a yield check.

questions.q: A solid steel shaft 40 mm in diameter runs at 1500 rev/min. The allowable shear stress is 50 MPa. Find the maximum power the shaft can transmit.
questions.modelAnswer: From τmax = 16T/(πd³), the allowable torque is T = τπd³/16 = 50 × π × 40³/16 = 628,300 N mm, or 628 N m. The angular speed is ω = 1500 × 2π/60 = 157.1 rad/s. The power is P = Tω = 628.3 × 157.1 = 98,700 W, about 98.7 kW. In practice, a stress concentration at keyways and a fatigue factor would reduce this value.

questions.q: A simply supported beam with a 100 mm wide × 200 mm deep rectangular section carries a maximum bending moment of 20 kN m. Find the second moment of area and the maximum bending stress.
markScheme: σ = My/I = 20 × 10⁶ × 100/66.7 × 10⁶ = 30 MPa (tension at the bottom and compression at the top for sagging)
questions.modelAnswer: The second moment of area about the centroidal axis is I = bd³/12 = 100 × 200³/12 = 66.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The extreme fibres are y = 100 mm from the neutral axis. Converting the moment to N mm, σmax = My/I = 20 × 10⁶ × 100/66.7 × 10⁶ = 30 MPa. Under sagging, the bottom fibre is in tension and the top fibre in compression. As a check, Z = bd²/6 = 666,667 mm³ gives the same 30 MPa.

questions.q: At a section where V = 30 kN, a 100 mm × 200 mm rectangular beam is under shear. Find the average and maximum shear stresses, and the shear stress 50 mm above the neutral axis.
markScheme: τmax = 1.5τ_avg = 2.25 MPa at the neutral axis
questions.modelAnswer: The average shear stress is V/A = 30,000/20,000 = 1.5 MPa. The distribution across a rectangle is parabolic, so the maximum, at the neutral axis, is 1.5 times the average: 2.25 MPa. At 50 mm above the neutral axis, the area above that level is 100 × 50 mm, with its centroid 75 mm from the neutral axis, so Q = 375,000 mm³. Then τ = VQ/(Ib) = 30,000 × 375,000/(66.7 × 10⁶ × 100) = 1.69 MPa, which is three quarters of the maximum, as the parabola predicts.

questions.q: A steel cantilever 2 m long (E = 200 GPa, I = 10 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carries a 5 kN load at its free end. Find the tip deflection and the tip slope.
questions.modelAnswer: EI = 200,000 N/mm² × 10 × 10⁶ mm⁴ = 2 × 10¹² N mm². The tip deflection of a cantilever with an end load is δ = PL³/(3EI) = 5000 × 2000³/(3 × 2 × 10¹²) = 6.67 mm. The tip slope is θ = PL²/(2EI) = 5000 × 2000²/(4 × 10¹²) = 0.005 rad, about 0.29°. Working in N and mm throughout avoids unit errors.

questions.q: A 40 mm diameter solid steel rod (E = 200 GPa) is used as a strut 1.5 m long, fixed at its base and free at its top. Find the Euler buckling load and the corresponding stress. How would the load change if the top were pinned instead?
markScheme: L_e = 2L = 3000 mm, so P_cr = π²EI/L_e² = 27.6 kN
Fixed–pinned: L_e ≈ 0.7L = 1050 mm, so P_cr ≈ 225 kN (about 8 times higher)
questions.modelAnswer: I = π × 40⁴/64 = 125,700 mm⁴ and A = 1257 mm². A fixed–free strut has effective length 2L = 3000 mm, so P_cr = π² × 200,000 × 125,700/3000² = 27.6 kN. The corresponding stress is 22 MPa, so buckling is elastic and well below yield. If the top were pinned, L_e ≈ 0.7 × 1500 = 1050 mm, giving P_cr = π² × 200,000 × 125,700/1050² ≈ 225 kN, about eight times higher. End restraint matters a great deal.

questions.q: Find the degree of static indeterminacy of: (a) a plane truss with 13 members and 8 joints on one pin and one roller; (b) a single-bay portal frame (three members, rigid knees) with both feet fixed.
markScheme: So the frame is indeterminate to the third degree (equivalently, an open tree structure with 6 reactions and 3 equilibrium equations)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For a pin-jointed plane truss, i = m + r − 2j = 13 + 3 − 16 = 0. The truss is statically determinate, provided its arrangement is stable.

(b) For a rigid-jointed plane frame, i = 3m + r − 3j. With three members, four joints (two feet and two knees) and six reactions (three at each fixed foot), i = 9 + 6 − 12 = 3. Equivalently, the frame is an open tree with six reactions and three equilibrium equations. It is indeterminate to the third degree, so three compatibility conditions are needed.

questions.q: A continuous beam ABC is fixed at A and C and continuous over support B. AB is 6 m long and BC is 4 m long, with constant EI. Find the distribution factors at B for moment distribution, and explain what the carry-over factor does.
markScheme: Stiffness of a member with a fixed far end = 4EI/L
Carry-over ½: a moment applied at the near end induces half that moment, with the same sign, at a fixed far end
questions.modelAnswer: Both far ends are fixed, so each member's rotational stiffness at B is 4EI/L. This gives k_BA = 4EI/6 = 0.667EI and k_BC = 4EI/4 = EI. The distribution factors are each member's share of the total stiffness: DF_BA = 0.667/1.667 = 0.40 and DF_BC = 0.60. Any out-of-balance moment at B is shared between the members in these proportions. The carry-over factor of ½ means that the balancing moment given to each member induces half that moment, with the same sign, at the fixed far end.

questions.q: A critical point on a bracket made from steel with σy = 250 MPa is in plane stress, with σx = 120 MPa, σy = −40 MPa and τxy = 50 MPa. (a) Find the principal stresses and the orientation of the principal planes. (b) Find the maximum in-plane shear stress and the absolute maximum shear stress. (c) Find the normal and shear stress on a plane whose normal is at 30° anticlockwise from x. (d) Find the factor of safety against yield using the Tresca and von Mises criteria, and comment on the difference.
markScheme: tan 2θp = 100/160, so θp = 16.0° anticlockwise from x to σ₁
τmax in-plane = R = 94.3 MPa; absolute = (σ₁ − σ₂)/2 = 94.3 MPa, since σ₃ = 0 lies between them
Tresca: σ₁ − σ₂ = 188.7 MPa, so FoS = 1.32
von Mises: σvm = √(σ₁² − σ₁σ₂ + σ₂²) = 168.2 MPa, so FoS = 1.49
Comment: Tresca is more conservative, by up to about 15%; von Mises fits ductile test data better
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The centre of Mohr's circle is at C = (σx + σy)/2 = 40 MPa. The radius is R = √[((σx − σy)/2)² + τxy²] = √(80² + 50²) = 94.3 MPa. The principal stresses are σ₁ = 40 + 94.3 = 134.3 MPa and σ₂ = 40 − 94.3 = −54.3 MPa, and the out-of-plane stress is σ₃ = 0. From tan 2θp = 2τxy/(σx − σy) = 100/160, 2θp = 32.0°, so σ₁ acts at 16.0° anticlockwise from the x axis and σ₂ at 106.0°.

(b) The maximum in-plane shear stress equals R = 94.3 MPa, on planes at 45° to the principal planes (61.0° and −29.0° from x). Because σ₃ = 0 lies between σ₁ and σ₂, the absolute maximum shear stress is also (σ₁ − σ₂)/2 = 94.3 MPa.

(c) For θ = 30° (2θ = 60°):
σ = 40 + 80 cos 60° + 50 sin 60° = 40 + 40 + 43.3 = 123.3 MPa
τ = −80 sin 60° + 50 cos 60° = −69.3 + 25 = −44.3 MPa
As a check, the plane is 14° from the σ₁ plane, so its normal stress should be slightly below σ₁, which it is.

(d) Tresca: yield when σmax − σmin = σy. Here 134.3 − (−54.3) = 188.7 MPa, so the factor of safety is 250/188.7 = 1.32.
von Mises: σvm = √(134.3² − 134.3 × (−54.3) + 54.3²) = 168.2 MPa. The same value comes from √(σx² − σxσy + σy² + 3τxy²) = √(14,400 + 4800 + 1600 + 7500) = 168.2 MPa. The factor of safety is 250/168.2 = 1.49.
The difference is about 12%. Tresca's hexagon lies inside the von Mises ellipse, and the gap is largest for shear-dominated states like this one, with principal stresses of opposite sign. Test data for ductile steels usually lie closer to von Mises, but Tresca is simpler and conservative. Both factors are fairly low for a bracket, so a designer should also consider fatigue and stress concentrations.

questions.q: A short compression member consists of a solid steel rod (area 1000 mm², E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /°C) inside a copper tube (area 1500 mm², E = 110 GPa, α = 17 × 10⁻⁶ /°C). Both are 500 mm long and are bonded to rigid end plates. (a) An axial compressive load of 100 kN is applied through the plates. Find the stress in each material and the shortening. (b) With no load, the assembly is then heated by 50 °C. Find the thermal stresses. (c) Find the final stresses when the load and the temperature rise act together, and state which material is closer to its limit if the yield stresses are 250 MPa for steel and 70 MPa for copper.
markScheme: (a) Compatibility: equal strain, so σs/Es = σc/Ec
Equilibrium: σs As + σc Ac = 100 kN
σs = P Es/(Es As + Ec Ac) = 54.8 MPa compression; σc = 30.1 MPa compression
(b) Copper expands more, so it goes into compression and steel into tension, with equal forces: σs As = σc Ac
Compatibility: σs/Es + αs ΔT = −σc/Ec + αc ΔT
σs = 22.6 MPa tension and σc = 15.1 MPa compression
Utilisation: steel 13% of yield, copper 65%, so copper is critical
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The rigid plates force equal strains in both materials, so σs/Es = σc/Ec and σs = (200/110)σc = 1.818σc. Equilibrium requires σs × 1000 + σc × 1500 = 100,000 N, so σc(1818 + 1500) = 100,000.
σc = 30.1 MPa and σs = 54.8 MPa, both compressive.
The shortening is σs L/Es = 54.8 × 500/200,000 = 0.137 mm.

(b) Free, the copper would expand more than the steel. Bonded together, the copper is held back, putting it in compression, and the steel is stretched into tension. With no external load, the internal forces balance: σs × 1000 = σc × 1500, so σc = (2/3)σs. Compatibility requires a common final strain:
σs/200,000 + 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 50 = −σc/110,000 + 17 × 10⁻⁶ × 50
σs(1/200,000 + 0.667/110,000) = 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 50 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴
σs = 22.6 MPa (tension) and σc = 15.1 MPa (compression).
The common strain is 7.13 × 10⁻⁴, an extension of 0.357 mm.

(c) The behaviour is linear, so the two cases can be superposed:
Steel: −54.8 + 22.6 = −32.2 MPa (compression)
Copper: −30.1 − 15.1 = −45.2 MPa (compression)
Check: 32.2 × 1000 + 45.2 × 1500 = 100,000 N. ✓
The steel is at 32.2/250 = 13% of yield and the copper at 45.2/70 = 65%, so the copper is critical even though it carries the lower stress under mechanical load alone. Heating moves load from the steel onto the copper. Designs of mixed-material members must check combined load cases, not each one separately.

questions.q: A drive shaft must transmit 30 kW at 600 rev/min. The proposed design is a hollow steel tube with 60 mm outer and 40 mm inner diameter, 2 m long, with G = 80 GPa. (a) Find the torque. (b) Find the maximum shear stress and the angle of twist in degrees. (c) Find the diameter of a solid shaft with the same maximum shear stress, and compare the masses of the two designs. (d) Explain physically why the hollow shaft is more efficient.
markScheme: Areas: solid 2442 mm² against hollow 1571 mm²
Hollow is about 64% of the mass of the solid shaft (a 36% saving)
Stress is proportional to radius; core material is lightly stressed and adds little to J
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ω = 600 × 2π/60 = 62.83 rad/s, so T = P/ω = 30,000/62.83 = 477 N m.

(b) J = π(60⁴ − 40⁴)/32 = π(12.96 × 10⁶ − 2.56 × 10⁶)/32 = 1.021 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The maximum shear stress, at the outer surface, is τmax = T r_o/J = 477,500 × 30/1.021 × 10⁶ = 14.0 MPa. This is a modest value, so the shaft is far from yield, with plenty of margin for fatigue at keyways. The angle of twist is θ = TL/(GJ) = 477,500 × 2000/(80,000 × 1.021 × 10⁶) = 0.0117 rad, which is 0.67°, inside a typical limit of about 1° per metre or less.

(c) For a solid shaft with τmax = 14.0 MPa, d = (16T/πτ)^(1/3) = (16 × 477,500/(π × 14.03))^(1/3) = 55.8 mm. The cross-sectional areas are π × 55.8²/4 = 2442 mm² for the solid shaft and π(60² − 40²)/4 = 1571 mm² for the hollow one. For the same material and length, the hollow shaft weighs 64% as much, a saving of about 36%. Its outer diameter is only 4 mm larger.

(d) In elastic torsion, shear strain and stress grow linearly from zero at the axis. Material near the centre is lightly stressed, and because J depends on r⁴ it adds very little to the strength or stiffness. Removing the core saves mass while the highly stressed, high-leverage outer material is kept. The limits are practical ones: manufacturing cost, and local buckling of very thin walls.

questions.q: A stepped steel shaft ABC is fixed rigidly at both ends, A and C. Segment AB is solid, 50 mm in diameter and 0.6 m long. Segment BC is solid, 40 mm in diameter and 0.4 m long. A torque of 2.0 kN m is applied at the step B. G = 80 GPa. Lead engineer Hamid Rahimi asks you to: (a) explain why the problem is statically indeterminate and set up the governing equations; (b) find the reaction torques at A and C; (c) find the maximum shear stress in each segment; (d) find the rotation of section B; (e) recommend, with justification, a single change that would equalise the peak stresses.
markScheme: Two unknown reactions T_A and T_C, but only one equilibrium equation: T_A + T_C = 2.0 kN m
Compatibility: φ_B from AB equals φ_B from BC, so T_A L_AB/(G J_AB) = T_C L_BC/(G J_BC)
τ_BC = 60.6 MPa (higher despite the lower torque)
φ_B = T_A L/(GJ) = 0.0151 rad = 0.87°, and the check from BC agrees
The torque divides in proportion to stiffness, while stress depends on d³

Recommendation with a quantitative argument. Both segments twist through the same φ_B, so τ = G φ_B r/L and the stresses are equal only when d/L is the same for both. Enlarging BC lowers both stresses but makes them diverge (e.g. 42.5 mm gives 45.7 and 58.2 MPa). Valid fixes: move B so that L_BC/L_AB = 0.8 (L_AB ≈ 0.56 m, both ≈ 54 MPa), or enlarge AB to 60 mm (both ≈ 36 MPa)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The fixed ends give two unknown reaction torques, T_A and T_C, but axial moment equilibrium gives only one equation: T_A + T_C = 2.0 kN m. The extra condition comes from compatibility. Section B must rotate by the same angle whether you work it out from A through AB or from C through CB:
T_A L_AB/(G J_AB) = T_C L_BC/(G J_BC).

(b) J_AB = π × 50⁴/32 = 613,600 mm⁴ and J_BC = π × 40⁴/32 = 251,300 mm⁴. The torsional stiffnesses are in the ratio (J_AB/L_AB)/(J_BC/L_BC) = (613,600/600)/(251,300/400) = 1022.7/628.3 = 1.628. The applied torque divides in proportion to stiffness:
T_A = 2.0 × 1.628/2.628 = 1.239 kN m and T_C = 0.761 kN m.

(c) Maximum shear stresses, from τ = 16T/(πd³):
τ_AB = 16 × 1.239 × 10⁶/(π × 50³) = 50.5 MPa
τ_BC = 16 × 0.761 × 10⁶/(π × 40³) = 60.6 MPa
The thinner segment carries less torque but is more highly stressed: stress goes as 1/d³, while torque share goes as d⁴/L.

(d) φ_B = T_A L_AB/(G J_AB) = 1.239 × 10⁶ × 600/(80,000 × 613,600) = 0.0151 rad = 0.87°. From the other side, 0.761 × 10⁶ × 400/(80,000 × 251,300) = 0.0151 rad, which agrees.

(e) Both segments twist through the same angle φ_B, and τ = G φ_B r/L, so the peak stresses are equal only when d/L is the same for both segments. Equivalently, τ_BC/τ_AB = (d_BC/d_AB)(L_AB/L_BC) = (40/50)(600/400) = 1.2 at present.
Enlarging BC does not help. With d_BC = 42.5 mm, J_BC = 320,300 mm⁴, the stiffness ratio becomes 1022.7/800.8 = 1.277, giving T_A = 1.122 kN m and T_C = 0.878 kN m. The stresses become 45.7 and 58.2 MPa: both fall, but stiffening BC draws torque into it and the gap widens (the ratio rises to 1.275).
Two changes do equalise the stresses. Moving B so that L_BC/L_AB = d_BC/d_AB = 0.80 gives L_AB ≈ 0.56 m and L_BC ≈ 0.44 m, with both segments at about 54 MPa; the step moves about 45 mm towards A. Alternatively, enlarging AB to 60 mm (d/L = 0.1 for both) gives T_A = 1.543 kN m and T_C = 0.457 kN m, with both segments at about 36 MPa, at the cost of 44% more mass in AB.
I would enlarge AB to 60 mm if the extra mass is acceptable, because it lowers the peak stress by 40%; relocating B equalises the stresses with no extra material but only cuts the peak to about 54 MPa. Either way, check the fillet stress concentration at the step B.

questions.q: A cast aluminium beam has a T-section: a flange 120 mm wide × 20 mm thick, on top of a web 20 mm thick × 100 mm deep (overall depth 120 mm). It is simply supported over 3.0 m and carries a uniformly distributed load of 5 kN/m, including self-weight. (a) Locate the neutral axis and find the second moment of area. (b) Find the maximum bending moment. (c) Find the maximum tensile and compressive bending stresses and where they occur. (d) Client Mei Chen asks whether turning the beam upside down would be better if the alloy's allowable tensile stress is 60 MPa. Advise her.
markScheme: Centroid from the bottom: ȳ = (2400 × 110 + 2000 × 50)/4400 = 82.7 mm
Mmax = wL²/8 = 5 × 9/8 = 5.625 kN m at midspan
Bottom (tension) = 5.625 × 10⁶ × 82.7/5.674 × 10⁶ = 82.0 MPa > 60 MPa, so it fails the check
Inverted: tension at the flange = 37.0 MPa < 60, compression at the web tip 82.0 MPa (check against compressive allowable and local buckling)
Advice: invert, or deepen or alter the section; note the lateral stability of the web in compression
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Measure from the bottom of the web. The flange has area 120 × 20 = 2400 mm² with its centroid at 110 mm. The web has area 20 × 100 = 2000 mm² with its centroid at 50 mm.
ȳ = (2400 × 110 + 2000 × 50)/4400 = 82.7 mm from the bottom, which is 37.3 mm below the top.
Using the parallel-axis theorem:
I_flange = 120 × 20³/12 + 2400 × (110 − 82.7)² = 0.080 × 10⁶ + 1.786 × 10⁶ = 1.866 × 10⁶ mm⁴
I_web = 20 × 100³/12 + 2000 × (82.7 − 50)² = 1.667 × 10⁶ + 2.141 × 10⁶ = 3.808 × 10⁶ mm⁴
I = 5.67 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

(b) Mmax = wL²/8 = 5 × 3²/8 = 5.625 kN m (sagging) at midspan, where the shear force is zero.

(c) Under sagging, the top is in compression and the bottom in tension:
σ_top = 5.625 × 10⁶ × 37.3/5.674 × 10⁶ = 37.0 MPa (compression), at the top of the flange
σ_bottom = 5.625 × 10⁶ × 82.7/5.674 × 10⁶ = 82.0 MPa (tension), at the tip of the web
Both occur at midspan.

(d) The tensile stress of 82.0 MPa exceeds the 60 MPa allowable, so the beam as drawn fails the check. Inverted, with the flange at the bottom, the extreme distances swap. Tension then occurs in the flange at 37.0 MPa, which is acceptable, and compression of 82.0 MPa occurs at the web tip. Cast alloys are usually stronger in compression, so inverting the beam is likely to work if the compressive allowable is above 82 MPa. Ms Chen should also check that the slender web tip in compression is restrained against local and lateral-torsional buckling. If it is not, a deeper or more symmetrical section is the safer choice.

questions.q: A beam ABC is simply supported at A and B, which are 6 m apart, and overhangs 2 m from B to C. It carries a uniform load of 10 kN/m over AB and a 20 kN point load at C. (a) Find the support reactions. (b) Sketch and describe the shear force and bending moment diagrams, giving key values. (c) Find the maximum sagging and hogging moments and the point of contraflexure. (d) Find the elastic section modulus needed for an allowable bending stress of 165 MPa.
markScheme: Shear: +23.3 at A, falling linearly to −36.7 just left of B, jump to +20.0, constant to C
V = 0 at x = 2.33 m from A
M_max sagging = 23.3²/(2 × 10) = 27.2 kN m at x = 2.33 m
M_B = −20 × 2 = −40 kN m (hogging), linear to zero at C
Contraflexure: 23.33x − 5x² = 0, so x = 4.67 m from A
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Taking moments about A: 6R_B = (10 × 6) × 3 + 20 × 8 = 180 + 160 = 340, so R_B = 56.7 kN. Vertical equilibrium gives R_A = 60 + 20 − 56.7 = 23.3 kN.
Check, moments about B: 23.3 × 6 = 140 = 60 × 3 − 20 × 2. ✓

(b) Shear force (positive upward on the left of a section):
- V = +23.3 kN at A, falling at 10 kN/m to 23.3 − 60 = −36.7 kN just left of B
- The reaction at B steps it up by 56.7 to +20.0 kN, which stays constant to C, where the point load returns it to zero
- V crosses zero at x = 23.3/10 = 2.33 m from A
Bending moment:
- Parabolic over AB: M(x) = 23.33x − 5x²
- Zero at A, a maximum where V = 0, then decreasing to M_B = 23.33 × 6 − 5 × 36 = −40 kN m
- Linear over BC from −40 kN m to zero at C (slope +20 kN m per m)

(c) The maximum sagging moment is 23.33 × 2.33 − 5 × 2.33² = 27.2 kN m at 2.33 m from A. The maximum hogging moment is 40 kN m at support B. The point of contraflexure is where 23.33x − 5x² = 0 on AB, at x = 4.67 m from A. Hogging continues from there over the overhang.

(d) The design moment is the larger magnitude, 40 kN m. The required section modulus is Z ≥ M/σ_allow = 40 × 10⁶/165 = 2.42 × 10⁵ mm³, or 242 cm³. A symmetric I-section with at least this elastic modulus would be chosen, and then checked for shear (the maximum is 36.7 kN, just left of B) and for deflection of the overhang.

questions.q: A steel I-beam is 200 mm deep overall. Its flanges are 100 mm wide × 12 mm thick, and its web is 8 mm thick. At one section it carries a vertical shear force of 80 kN. (a) Find the second moment of area about the neutral axis. (b) Find the shear stress at the neutral axis, in the web at the web–flange junction, and in the flange at the junction. (c) Find what proportion of the shear force the web carries. (d) Explain why designers often use τ ≈ V/(d t_w) as a quick check.
markScheme: τ_flange,junction (b = 100) = 3.6 MPa: a sudden jump in width
Web force = t_w h_w[τ_j + (2/3)(τ_NA − τ_j)] = 75.6 kN
So the web carries about 94% of V
V/(d t_w) = 50 MPa is close to the mean web stress; it is simple and adequate for standard rolled sections
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Treat the section as a 100 × 200 mm rectangle minus two voids, together 92 mm wide × 176 mm deep:
I = (100 × 200³ − 92 × 176³)/12 = (800 × 10⁶ − 501.6 × 10⁶)/12 = 24.87 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

(b) The neutral axis is at mid-depth. For one flange, Q = 100 × 12 × (100 − 6) = 112,800 mm³. Adding the half-web above the neutral axis, 8 × 88 with its centroid at 44 mm, gives Q_NA = 112,800 + 30,976 = 143,776 mm³.
- At the neutral axis (b = 8 mm): τ = 80,000 × 143,776/(24.87 × 10⁶ × 8) = 57.8 MPa
- In the web at the junction (b = 8 mm): τ = 80,000 × 112,800/(24.87 × 10⁶ × 8) = 45.4 MPa
- In the flange at the junction (b = 100 mm): τ = 45.4 × 8/100 = 3.6 MPa
The sudden drop reflects the change in width. In reality the flanges mainly carry horizontal shear flow.

(c) Over the web's height h_w = 176 mm, the shear stress is parabolic, rising from 45.4 MPa at each junction to 57.8 MPa at the neutral axis. The area under a parabola above its base value is two-thirds of the rectangle that encloses it, so the web force is
8 × 176 × [45.4 + (2/3)(57.8 − 45.4)] = 1408 × 53.7 = 75.6 kN.
That is about 94% of the 80 kN shear.

(d) Since the web carries almost all the shear at a nearly uniform stress (45 to 58 MPa), dividing V by the web area gives a good estimate. Using the full depth, V/(d t_w) = 80,000/(200 × 8) = 50 MPa, which is close to the mean web stress of 53.7 MPa. The approximation is simple and adequate for rolled I-sections, and design codes take a similar approach with a defined shear area. It would be poor for sections with thick webs or shallow flanges.

questions.q: A timber T-beam for a footbridge is made by nailing a 150 mm wide × 50 mm deep flange plank on top of a 50 mm wide × 150 mm deep web plank, giving an overall depth of 200 mm. The maximum shear force is 2 kN. Each nail can safely carry 800 N in shear, and nails are driven in a single row. (a) Locate the neutral axis and find I. (b) Find the shear flow at the flange–web interface. (c) Find the maximum nail spacing. (d) Find the maximum shear stress in the timber and say where it occurs. (e) Contractor Leo Marsh proposes doubling the spacing near midspan. Comment.
markScheme: Areas 7500 mm² each; centroids at 175 mm and 75 mm from the bottom; ȳ = 125 mm
Q of flange about the NA = 7500 × 50 = 375,000 mm³
τmax at the neutral axis in the web: Q = 50 × 125 × 62.5 = 390,625 mm³
Spacing can increase where V is smaller, since q ∝ V
For a midspan point load V does not reduce; for a uniform load V falls towards midspan, so larger spacing is acceptable there, subject to a minimum or code maximum spacing
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Measure from the bottom of the web. The web, 50 × 150 = 7500 mm², has its centroid at 75 mm. The flange, 150 × 50 = 7500 mm², has its centroid at 175 mm. Since the areas are equal, ȳ = 125 mm from the bottom, which is 75 mm below the top.
I = 150 × 50³/12 + 7500 × 50² + 50 × 150³/12 + 7500 × 50² = 1.56 × 10⁶ + 18.75 × 10⁶ + 14.06 × 10⁶ + 18.75 × 10⁶ = 53.1 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

(b) The nails must transfer the horizontal shear between the flange and the web. The first moment of the flange about the neutral axis is Q = 7500 × (175 − 125) = 375,000 mm³, so
q = VQ/I = 2000 × 375,000/53.1 × 10⁶ = 14.1 N/mm.

(c) Each nail carries q × s, so s ≤ 800/14.1 = 56.7 mm. Specify 55 mm centres in the region of maximum shear.

(d) The maximum shear stress occurs at the neutral axis, which lies in the web 125 mm above its base. Taking the area below: Q = 50 × 125 × 62.5 = 390,625 mm³, and b = 50 mm:
τ = 2000 × 390,625/(53.1 × 10⁶ × 50) = 0.29 MPa.
This is low compared with typical shear strengths for structural timber, but the nails are the critical element.

(e) The shear flow is proportional to V, so the spacing can be increased where the shear force is lower. Under a uniform load, V falls linearly to zero at midspan, and doubling the spacing where V ≤ 1 kN is justified. Under a concentrated load at midspan, such as a maintenance cart, V stays at its full value up to the load, and doubling the spacing there would overload the nails. Mr Marsh's proposal is acceptable only for the parts of the span where the design shear, including moving loads, is at most half the maximum. The spacing should also stay within the code limits that control the slip between the planks.

questions.q: A steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa, I = 40 × 10⁶ mm⁴) is 3 m long. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 4 kN/m along its whole length and a 6 kN point load at its free end. (a) Using superposition of standard results, find the tip deflection and the tip slope. (b) Confirm the deflection due to the point load by double integration. (c) If the serviceability limit for a cantilever is span/180, does the beam pass?
markScheme: Double integration from the fixed end: EI y″ = −P(L − x)
Boundary conditions y(0) = 0 and y′(0) = 0, giving y(L) = −PL³/(3EI)
Limit L/180 = 16.7 mm > 11.8 mm, so it passes
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) First find EI in consistent units: 200 × 10⁶ kN/m² × 40 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴ = 8000 kN m². Superposition is valid because the response is linear.
Uniform load: δ = wL⁴/(8EI) = 4 × 3⁴/(8 × 8000) = 0.00506 m = 5.06 mm
End load: δ = PL³/(3EI) = 6 × 27/(3 × 8000) = 0.00675 m = 6.75 mm
Total tip deflection = 11.8 mm, downwards.
Tip slope: θ = wL³/(6EI) + PL²/(2EI) = 4 × 27/48,000 + 6 × 9/16,000 = 0.00225 + 0.00338 = 0.00563 rad, about 0.32°.

(b) Put the origin at the fixed end with y positive upwards. Under the end load alone, the moment at x is M = −P(L − x), which is hogging. So:
EI y″ = −P(L − x)
EI y′ = −P(Lx − x²/2) + C₁
EI y = −P(Lx²/2 − x³/6) + C₁x + C₂
At the fixed end, y(0) = 0 and y′(0) = 0, so C₁ = C₂ = 0. At x = L: EI y = −P(L³/2 − L³/6) = −PL³/3. That confirms δ = PL³/(3EI) = 6.75 mm.

(c) The limit is 3000/180 = 16.7 mm. The calculated 11.8 mm is within it, so the beam passes, with about 30% margin. The designer should check the strength separately: the root moment is 4 × 9/2 + 6 × 3 = 36 kN m. Long-term effects such as creep do not apply to steel, but any self-weight not already included in the 4 kN/m must be added.

questions.q: A simply supported steel beam AB spans 5 m. It carries a single 20 kN point load at 2 m from A, and EI = 8000 kN m². (a) Using Macaulay's method, derive the equation of the elastic curve. (b) Find the slope at A and the deflection under the load. (c) Find the position and value of the maximum deflection. (d) A second, identical load is to be added at 2 m from B. Use symmetry and superposition to find the new midspan deflection, and explain whether the maximum now occurs at midspan.
markScheme: y(2) = (16 − 64)/8000 = −6.0 mm, which agrees with Pa²b²/(3EIL)
Maximum where y′ = 0 in x > 2: 6x² − 10(x − 2)² − 32 = 0, so x = 2.35 m
Second load: by symmetry, midspan deflection = 2 × (deflection at 2.5 m from one load) = 2 × 6.15 = 12.3 mm, and the maximum is at midspan by symmetry
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Moments about B: 5R_A = 20 × 3, so R_A = 12 kN and R_B = 8 kN. With x measured from A, y positive upwards and sagging positive:
EI y″ = 12x − 20⟨x − 2⟩
Integrating the bracket as a single unit, without expanding it:
EI y′ = 6x² − 10⟨x − 2⟩² + C₁
EI y = 2x³ − (10/3)⟨x − 2⟩³ + C₁x + C₂
At x = 0, y = 0, so C₂ = 0. At x = 5, y = 0: 2(125) − (10/3)(27) + 5C₁ = 0, so 250 − 90 + 5C₁ = 0 and C₁ = −32 kN m².

(b) The slope at A is θ_A = C₁/EI = −32/8000 = −0.004 rad (the beam slopes downwards).
Under the load at x = 2 the bracket term is zero: EI y = 16 − 64 = −48, so y = −0.006 m = 6.0 mm downwards.
Check: Pa²b²/(3EIL) = 20 × 4 × 9/(3 × 8000 × 5) = 6.0 mm. ✓

(c) The maximum lies in the longer segment, where y′ = 0 for x > 2:
6x² − 10(x − 2)² − 32 = 0
−4x² + 40x − 72 = 0, so x² − 10x + 18 = 0 and x = 5 − √7 = 2.35 m from A.
Then EI y = 2(2.354)³ − (10/3)(0.354)³ − 32(2.354) = 26.09 − 0.15 − 75.33 = −49.39, so y_max = 6.17 mm.
This matches the standard result √[(L² − a²)/3] = 2.65 m from B, and is only 3% more than the deflection under the load.

(d) At midspan (x = 2.5), the first load gives EI y = 2(15.625) − (10/3)(0.125) − 80 = −49.17, so y = 6.15 mm. The mirror-image second load gives the same value there. By superposition, the midspan deflection is 2 × 6.15 = 12.3 mm. The loading is now symmetrical, so the slope at midspan is zero and the maximum deflection occurs exactly there.

questions.q: A pin-ended steel strut 2.5 m long has a solid rectangular section 80 mm × 40 mm. It is braced at mid-height against buckling about its weak axis only. E = 200 GPa and σy = 250 MPa. (a) Find the second moments of area and radii of gyration about both principal axes. (b) Find the Euler load for buckling about each axis, with the appropriate effective lengths. (c) Find the governing buckling load and stress, and check whether Euler theory is valid. (d) Comment on the efficiency of this bracing arrangement, and on why the real failure load would be lower.
markScheme: Major axis: L_e = 2.5 m, so P_cr = 539 kN
σ_cr = 539,000/3200 = 168 MPa < 250 MPa; λ > λ_lim = π√(E/σy) = 88.9, so Euler applies
The two axes are equally critical, a balanced design
Imperfections, eccentricity and residual stress reduce the strength below Euler, especially near λ_lim; Perry–Robertson or code curves give a lower capacity
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A = 80 × 40 = 3200 mm².
Minor axis (bending across the 40 mm dimension): I = 80 × 40³/12 = 4.27 × 10⁵ mm⁴, r = 40/√12 = 11.5 mm.
Major axis: I = 40 × 80³/12 = 1.71 × 10⁶ mm⁴, r = 80/√12 = 23.1 mm.

(b) About the minor axis, the mid-height brace halves the effective length, so L_e = 1.25 m:
P_cr = π² × 200,000 × 4.27 × 10⁵/1250² = 539 kN.
About the major axis there is no intermediate restraint, so L_e = 2.5 m:
P_cr = π² × 200,000 × 1.71 × 10⁶/2500² = 539 kN.

(c) The two values are equal, because I differs by a factor of 4 and L_e² also differs by a factor of 4. The governing Euler load is 539 kN, and buckling is equally likely about either axis. The slenderness is 1250/11.5 = 2500/23.1 = 108 for both axes. The critical stress is 539,000/3200 = 168 MPa, below σy = 250 MPa. The transition slenderness is π√(200,000/250) = 88.9. Since λ = 108 is greater than this, elastic Euler buckling governs and the formula is valid.

(d) The bracing is well matched to the section. Halving the weak-axis length raises the minor-axis load fourfold, exactly balancing the two axes. More bracing about the weak axis alone would give no further benefit, because the major axis would then govern.
Real struts carry less than this. Initial out-of-straightness, eccentric load at the pins and residual stresses all cause bending as soon as load is applied, so the extreme fibre yields before P_E is reached. With λ = 108, only modestly above the transition value, this reduction is significant. A Perry–Robertson analysis or the Eurocode 3 buckling curves would give a design resistance well below 539 kN, before partial factors are applied.

questions.q: A two-span continuous beam ABC is simply supported at A, B and C, with AB = BC = 4 m and constant EI. It carries a uniform load of 15 kN/m over both spans. (a) State the degree of indeterminacy. (b) Using the flexibility (force) method with R_B as the redundant, find all three reactions. (c) Draw and describe the bending moment diagram, giving the hogging moment at B, the maximum sagging moment and its position, and the points of contraflexure. (d) Compare the maximum moment with that of two separate simply supported 4 m spans, and discuss one advantage and one disadvantage of continuity.
markScheme: Four reactions (with horizontal at A) minus three equations = 1 degree
Release B: deflection at midspan of the 8 m beam under the uniform load = 5w(2L)⁴/(384EI)
Sagging maximum where V = 0: x = 22.5/15 = 1.5 m from A; M = 16.9 kN m (= 9wL²/128)
Contraflexure at x = 3.0 m from A (and C)
Simple spans: wL²/8 = 30 kN m sagging; the peak magnitude is the same but continuity cuts sagging by 44% and reduces deflection
Advantage: stiffer, less deflection, redundancy. Disadvantage: sensitive to settlement, hogging needs top reinforcement or splices
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) There are four reaction components: vertical reactions at A, B and C, and a horizontal reaction at A. There are three equilibrium equations, so the beam is indeterminate to the first degree.

(b) Remove support B to leave a simply supported 8 m beam. Under the uniform load, its midspan deflection is δ_w = 5w(8)⁴/(384EI). An upward point load R_B at midspan lifts the beam by R_B(8)³/(48EI). Compatibility requires zero deflection at B:
R_B × 512/48 = 5 × 15 × 4096/384
R_B = 5 × 15 × 8 × 48/384 = 75 kN, which is 1.25wL.
By symmetry, R_A = R_C = (15 × 8 − 75)/2 = 22.5 kN, or 0.375wL.

(c) For span AB, M(x) = 22.5x − 7.5x².
- At B (x = 4): M_B = 90 − 120 = −30 kN m (hogging), which is wL²/8
- Maximum sagging moment where V = 22.5 − 15x = 0, at x = 1.5 m from A: M = 33.75 − 16.88 = 16.9 kN m, which is 9wL²/128
- Point of contraflexure where M = 0: x = 22.5/7.5 = 3.0 m from A, so 1.0 m either side of B
The diagram is symmetrical about B: parabolic sagging lobes in each span and a hogging peak of 30 kN m over the central support.

(d) Two separate simply supported 4 m spans would each have a sagging maximum of wL²/8 = 30 kN m, and reactions of 30 kN at each end, giving 60 kN at the shared support. Continuity keeps the peak magnitude at 30 kN m but moves it to hogging over B, and it cuts the sagging moment by 44%. The midspan deflection also drops sharply, roughly 60% less than for a simple span.
One advantage is the greater stiffness and redundancy: if a hinge forms at B, load can redistribute, which gives reserve plastic capacity. One disadvantage is that indeterminacy makes the beam sensitive to support settlement and temperature gradients, which induce extra moments. The hogging region also needs top reinforcement in concrete, or moment-resisting splices in steel.

questions.q: A wall bracket is a pin-jointed truss of two members. Member AC is horizontal and 3 m long, pinned to the wall at A. Member BC is inclined and pinned to the wall at B, 4 m directly below A. A vertical load of 30 kN hangs at C. Both members have A = 800 mm² and E = 200 GPa. (a) Find the member forces. (b) Using the unit load method, find the vertical deflection of C. (c) Find the horizontal deflection of C. (d) Find the total displacement, and explain the physical meaning of the product N n in the virtual work sum.
markScheme: Joint C vertical: F_BC × 4/5 = 30, so F_BC = 37.5 kN compression
Vertical unit load at C: n_BC = −1.25 and n_AC = +0.75
AE = 800 × 200,000 N = 160 MN, giving δ_v = 1.78 mm downward
Horizontal unit load at C: n_AC = +1 and n_BC = 0
δ_h = 22.5 × 10³ × 3000/(160 × 10⁶) = 0.42 mm away from the wall
N n L/(AE): the real extension of each member multiplied by the internal virtual force; the unit load's external virtual work equals the internal virtual work
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) B is 4 m below A and C is 3 m out from the wall, so BC = 5 m, with direction cosines 3/5 horizontal and 4/5 vertical. At joint C, the 30 kN load must be supported by the vertical component of BC, which pushes up and out as a strut:
F_BC × 4/5 = 30, so F_BC = 37.5 kN (compression).
Its horizontal component, 37.5 × 3/5 = 22.5 kN, pushes C away from the wall. AC must pull C back, so F_AC = 22.5 kN (tension).

(b) A unit vertical load at C gives the same pattern scaled by 1/30: n_BC = −1.25 and n_AC = +0.75. With AE = 800 × 200,000 = 1.6 × 10⁸ N:
δ_v = Σ N n L/(AE) = [(−37,500)(−1.25)(5000) + (22,500)(0.75)(3000)]/1.6 × 10⁸
= (234.4 × 10⁶ + 50.6 × 10⁶)/1.6 × 10⁸ = 1.78 mm, downwards.

(c) A unit horizontal load at C, directed away from the wall, must be resisted entirely by the horizontal tie. The strut cannot help, because its vertical component would be unbalanced. So n_AC = +1 and n_BC = 0:
δ_h = 22,500 × 1 × 3000/1.6 × 10⁸ = 0.42 mm, away from the wall.
The answer is positive, so C moves in the direction of the unit load.

The term N L/(AE) is the real change in length of each member. Multiplying it by n, the internal force produced by a unit external load, gives the internal virtual work done as the virtual force system rides through the real deformations. Equating this to the external virtual work, 1 × δ, gives the displacement. The method is exact for linear elastic, small-displacement behaviour, and it avoids drawing a Williot displacement diagram.
